claim: The Drosophila ITP gene can generate three different peptide isoforms: ITP amidated (ITPa) and two ITP-like (ITPL1 and ITPL2) isoforms.
source: The Drosophila ITP gene can generate three different peptide isoforms: ITP amidated (ITPa) and two ITP-like (ITPL1 and ITPL2) isoforms.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by Figure 1A showing the gene structure and transcript variants.

claim: ITPa-producing neurons are activated and release ITPa during dehydration.
source: Moreover, we show that ITPa-producing neurons are activated and release ITPa during dehydration.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8 using CaLexA reporter and ITPa immunofluorescence measurements.

claim: Recombinant Drosophila ITPa inhibits diuretic peptide-induced renal tubule secretion ex vivo.
source: Furthermore, recombinant Drosophila ITPa inhibits diuretic peptide-induced renal tubule secretion ex vivo, thus confirming its role as an anti-diuretic hormone.
evidence: Demonstrated through Ramsay assay experiments shown in Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: Gyc76C is a bona fide Drosophila ITPa receptor.
source: Using a phylogenetic-driven approach, an ex vivo secretion assay and a heterologous mammalian cell-based assay, we identified and functionally characterized Gyc76C, a membrane guanylate cyclase, as a bona fide Drosophila ITPa receptor.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis (Figure 4B), ex vivo Ramsay assays (Figure 6E-F), and HEK293T cell-based assays (Figure 7).

claim: Gyc76C is highly expressed in larval and adult tissues associated with osmoregulation (renal tubules and rectum) and metabolic homeostasis (fat body).
source: Extensive anatomical mapping of Gyc76C reveals that it is highly expressed in larval and adult tissues associated with osmoregulation (renal tubules and rectum) and metabolic homeostasis (fat body).
evidence: Demonstrated through immunohistochemistry and GAL4 driver expression patterns shown in Figure 5.

claim: Knockdown of Gyc76C in renal tubules impacts tolerance to osmotic and ionic stresses.
source: Consistent with this expression, knockdown of Gyc76C in renal tubules impacts tolerance to osmotic and ionic stresses, whereas knockdown specifically in the fat body impacts feeding, nutrient homeostasis, and associated behaviors.
evidence: Shown through stress tolerance assays in Figure 11.

claim: Knockdown of Gyc76C in the fat body impacts feeding, nutrient homeostasis, and associated behaviors.
source: Consistent with this expression, knockdown of Gyc76C in renal tubules impacts tolerance to osmotic and ionic stresses, whereas knockdown specifically in the fat body impacts feeding, nutrient homeostasis, and associated behaviors.
evidence: Demonstrated through feeding assays, metabolite measurements, and behavioral tests shown in Figure 12.

claim: ITP derived its name from its first determined function in the locust Schistocerca gregaria, where it increases chloride transport across the ileum and acts as an anti-diuretic hormone.
source: ITP derived its name from its first determined function in the locust Schistocerca gregaria, where it increases chloride transport across the ileum and acts as an anti-diuretic hormone (Audsley et al., 1992b).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In Drosophila, ITP influences feeding, drinking, metabolism, and excretion.
source: In Drosophila, ITP influences feeding, drinking, metabolism, and excretion (Gáliková et al., 2018; Gáliková and Klepsatel, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ITP has a localized interneuronal role in the Drosophila circadian clock system.
source: Moreover, it has a localized interneuronal role in the Drosophila circadian clock system (Johard et al., 2009; Hermann-Luibl et al., 2014; Reinhard et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ITPa is a C-terminally amidated 73 amino acid neuropeptide.
source: ITPa is a C-terminally amidated 73 amino acid neuropeptide, while ITPL1 and ITPL2 are non-amidated and possess an alternate, extended C-terminus.
evidence: This is a structural characterization based on the gene structure shown in Figure 1A.

claim: ITPL1 and ITPL2 are non-amidated and possess an alternate, extended C-terminus.
source: ITPa is a C-terminally amidated 73 amino acid neuropeptide, while ITPL1 and ITPL2 are non-amidated and possess an alternate, extended C-terminus.
evidence: This is a structural characterization based on the gene structure shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Insect ITP is homologous to crustacean hyperglycemic hormone (CHH) and molt-inhibiting hormone (MIH).
source: Moreover, insect ITP is homologous to crustacean hyperglycemic hormone (CHH) and molt-inhibiting hormone (MIH), which together form a large family of multifunctional neuropeptides (Meredith et al., 1996; Dai et al., 2007; Drexler et al., 2007; Dircksen et al., 2008; Begum et al., 2009; Webster et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature and sequence alignment shown in Figure 4A.

claim: ITPa is produced by a small set of interneurons and NSC in the Drosophila brain and VNC.
source: ITPa is produced by a small set of interneurons and NSC in the Drosophila brain and VNC (Dircksen et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation and confirmed by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Bombyx ITPa and ITPL were found to activate G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) for pyrokinin and tachykinin neuropeptides, respectively.
source: Surprisingly, Bombyx ITPa and ITPL were found to activate G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) for pyrokinin and tachykinin neuropeptides, respectively (Nagai et al., 2014; Nagai-Okatani et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ITPL2 exerts anti-diuretic effects via the tachykinin receptor 99D (TkR99D) in a Drosophila tumor model.
source: Recently, ITPL2 was also shown to exert anti-diuretic effects via the tachykinin receptor 99D (TkR99D) in a Drosophila tumor model (Xu et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: ITPa is localized in at least seven bilateral pairs of neurons in the brain.
source: In agreement with previous reports (Dircksen et al., 2008; Kahsai et al., 2010; Zandawala et al., 2018b), ITPa is localized in at least seven bilateral pairs of neurons in the brain (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by citations and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: L-NSCITP co-express ITPa, tachykinin, short neuropeptide F (sNPF), and leucokinin (LK).
source: Amongst these are four pairs of lateral NSC, L-NSCITP also known as ipc-1 (Dircksen et al., 2008), or ALKs (de Haro et al., 2010), that co-express ITPa, tachykinin, short neuropeptide F (sNPF), and leucokinin (LK) (Kahsai et al., 2010; Zandawala et al., 2018b).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: L-NSCDH31 co-express diuretic hormone 31 (DH31) and ITPa.
source: Lastly, ITPa is weakly expressed in a pair of lateral NSC (also known as ipc-2a Dircksen et al., 2008). We demonstrate that these neurons (L-NSCDH31) co-express diuretic hormone 31 (DH31) (Figure 1B, Figure 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated through immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 2A.

claim: All ITPa brain neurons co-express ITPL1 (ITP-RC).
source: Interestingly, all ITPa brain neurons co-express ITPL1 (ITP-RC) (Figure 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated through GAL4 driver expression and immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 1B.

claim: ITPa expression in the VNC is comprised of only the abdominal ganglion efferent neurons (iag) which innervate the hindgut and rectum.
source: ITPa expression in the VNC is also sparse and is comprised of only the abdominal ganglion efferent neurons (iag) which innervate the hindgut and rectum (Figure 1C and D; Dircksen et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 1C and D.

claim: iag neurons co-express allatostatin-A (Ast-A) and crustacean cardioactive peptide (CCAP).
source: Interestingly, iag neurons co-express allatostatin-A (Ast-A) (Figure 2C, D) and crustacean cardioactive peptide (CCAP) (Figure 2E).
evidence: Demonstrated through immunohistochemistry shown in Figures 2C, D, and E.

claim: ITP is expressed in the trachea, Malpighian (renal) tubules (MTs), heart, fat body, and gut.
source: Surprisingly, this initial analysis revealed widespread expression of ITP across the fly (Figure 3A–D). In particular, ITP is expressed in the trachea, Malpighian (renal) tubules (MTs), heart, fat body, and gut (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: Demonstrated through single-nucleus transcriptome analysis shown in Figures 3B-D.

claim: ITPL1 (ITP-RC-T2A-GAL4 driven GFP) was detected in peripheral neurons that innervate the heart.
source: As is the case in Bombyx, ITPL1 (ITP-RC-T2A-GAL4 driven GFP) was detected in peripheral neurons that innervate the heart (Figure 3E).
evidence: Demonstrated through GAL4 driver expression shown in Figure 3E.

claim: ITPa immunoreactivity was detected in a pair of peripheral neurons which innervate the heart and alary muscle.
source: Like ITPL1, ITPa immunoreactivity was also detected in a pair of peripheral neurons which innervate the heart and alary muscle (Figure 3J), as well as in iag neuron axons that innervate the rectum (Figure 3K).
evidence: Demonstrated through immunohistochemistry shown in Figures 3J and K.

claim: ITPL2 is expressed in the heart muscles and the neighboring pericardial nephrocytes.
source: Thus, ITP-RD-T2A-GAL4 drives GFP expression in the heart muscles and the neighboring pericardial nephrocytes (Figure 3M), as well as in cells of the middle midgut (Figure 3N), posterior midgut (Figure 3O), ureter (Figure 3P), and trachea (Figure 3Q), but not the fat body (Figure 3R).
evidence: Demonstrated through GAL4 driver expression shown in Figures 3M-R.

claim: Neither PK2-R1, TkR99D, nor CG30340 are expressed in the epithelial cells of the rectal pad which mediate ion and water reabsorption.
source: Our analysis revealed that neither of the three candidate Drosophila receptors, PK2-R1, TkR99D, and CG30340, are expressed in the epithelial cells of the rectal pad which mediate ion and water reabsorption (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated through GAL4 driver expression analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Recombinant ITPa failed to activate both TkR99D and PK2-R1 heterologously expressed in mammalian CHO-K1 cells.
source: To test this experimentally, we generated recombinant ITPa for analysis of GPCR activation ex vivo. We found that recombinant ITPa failed to activate both TkR99D and PK2-R1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) heterologously expressed in mammalian CHO-K1 cells.
evidence: Demonstrated through cell-based assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: ITP/CHH/MIH-like genes are found in arthropods, nematodes, tardigrades, priapulid worms, and mollusks.
source: Our analyses retrieved ITP/CHH/MIH-like genes in arthropods, nematodes, tardigrades, priapulid worms, and mollusks (Figure 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated through BLAST and HMM-based searches and sequence alignment shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The six cysteines and a few amino acid residues adjacent to them are highly conserved in ITP precursor sequences.
source: A comparison of representative ITP precursor sequences from different phyla reveals that the six cysteines and a few amino acid residues adjacent to them are highly conserved (Figure 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated through sequence alignment shown in Figure 4A.

claim: ITP appears to be restricted to protostomian invertebrates and does not have orthologs in deuterostomian invertebrates and vertebrates.
source: Thus, ITP appears to be restricted to protostomian invertebrates and does not have orthologs in deuterostomian invertebrates and vertebrates.
evidence: Based on phylogenetic distribution analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis grouped mGC into six distinct clades.
source: Phylogenetic analysis grouped mGC into six distinct clades (Figure 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated through phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Two clades of mGC only contain receptors from protostomian invertebrates.
source: Importantly, we retrieved two clades which only contain receptors from protostomian invertebrates (Figure 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated through phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Gyc76C is more highly expressed than Gyc32E in MTs.
source: However, single-nucleus sequencing data indicate that Gyc76C is more highly expressed than Gyc32E in MTs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated through single-nucleus sequencing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Gyc76C-T2A-GAL4 drives GFP expression throughout the adult intestinal tract, including the anterior midgut, ureter (of renal tubules), and posterior midgut.
source: In males, Gyc76C-T2A-GAL4 drives GFP expression throughout the adult intestinal tract, including the anterior midgut (Figure 5B), ureter (of renal tubules) (Figure 5C), and posterior midgut (Figure 5D).
evidence: Demonstrated through GAL4 driver expression shown in Figures 5B-D.

claim: Gyc76C is highly expressed in the renal tubules, rectum, and adipocytes of the fat body.
source: Importantly, in agreement with the role of Drosophila ITP in regulating osmotic (Gáliková et al., 2018) and metabolic homeostasis (Gáliková and Klepsatel, 2022), Gyc76C is highly expressed in the renal tubules (Figure 5E), rectum (Figure 5F), and adipocytes of the fat body (Figure 5G).
evidence: Demonstrated through GAL4 driver expression shown in Figures 5E-G and supported by citations.

claim: There is a convergence of ITPa-immunolabeled axon terminations and Gyc76C expression in the anterior midgut and the rectal papillae in the rectum.
source: Moreover, we see a convergence of ITPa-immunolabeled axon terminations and Gyc76C expression in the anterior midgut (Figure 5H) and the rectal papillae in the rectum (Figure 5I), the latter of which are important for water reabsorption as first proposed nearly a century ago (Wigglesworth, 1932).
evidence: Demonstrated through immunohistochemistry shown in Figures 5H and I, and supported by citation.

claim: Gyc76C is broadly expressed in neurons throughout the brain and VNC.
source: Gyc76C is also broadly expressed in neurons throughout the brain (Figure 5J) and VNC (Figure 5K).
evidence: Demonstrated through GAL4 driver expression shown in Figures 5J and K.

claim: Gyc76C is expressed in glia clock cells and subsets of dorsal clock neurons.
source: Consistent with the role of ITP in regulating circadian rhythms, Gyc76C is expressed in glia clock cells (Figure 5L), and subsets of dorsal clock neurons (labeled with antibody against the clock protein Period) that are near the axon terminations of the clock neurons LNdITP and 5th-LNv (Figure 5M).
evidence: Demonstrated through immunohistochemistry shown in Figures 5L and M.

claim: Gyc76C is not expressed in male IPCs but is expressed in a subset of female IPCs.
source: Interestingly, Gyc76C is not expressed in male IPCs (labeled with antibody against DILP2) (Figure 5N) but is expressed in a subset of female IPCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated through immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 5N and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Gyc76C is not expressed in endocrine cells producing glucagon-like adipokinetic hormone (AKH) in either males or females.
source: However, Gyc76C is not expressed in endocrine cells producing glucagon-like adipokinetic hormone (AKH) in either males (Figure 5O) or females (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated through immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 5O and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Gyc76C is expressed in the corpora allata.
source: Interestingly, L-NSCDH31, which innervate the corpora allata, might utilize both DH31 and ITPa/ITPL1 to modulate juvenile hormone production since Gyc76C is expressed in the corpora allata (Figure 5O).
evidence: Demonstrated through immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 5O.

claim: Recombinant ITPa does not influence rates of secretion by unstimulated tubules.
source: Interestingly, recombinant ITPa does not influence rates of secretion by unstimulated tubules (Figure 6B).
evidence: Demonstrated through Ramsay assay shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Recombinant ITPa inhibits LK-stimulated secretion by MTs from w1118 flies.
source: Recombinant ITPa inhibits LK-stimulated secretion by MTs from w1118 flies (Figure 6C), indicating that stellate cell-driven diuresis is sensitive to this anti-diuretic hormone.
evidence: Demonstrated through Ramsay assay shown in Figure 6C.

claim: DH31-stimulated secretion was inhibited by recombinant ITPa.
source: Similarly, DH31-stimulated secretion was also inhibited by recombinant ITPa (Figure 6D), demonstrating that principal cells are also modulated by ITPa.
evidence: Demonstrated through Ramsay assay shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Knocking down expression of Gyc76C in stellate cells using c724-GAL4 abolished the anti-diuretic action of ITPa in LK-stimulated tubules.
source: Notably, knocking down expression of Gyc76C in stellate cells using c724-GAL4 abolished the anti-diuretic action of ITPa in LK-stimulated tubules (Figure 6E).
evidence: Demonstrated through Ramsay assay with genetic manipulation shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Knocking down expression of Gyc76C in principal cells using uro-GAL4 abolished the anti-diuretic action of ITPa in DH31-stimulated tubules.
source: Additionally, knocking down expression of Gyc76C in principal cells using uro-GAL4 abolished the anti-diuretic action of ITPa in DH31-stimulated tubules (Figure 6F).
evidence: Demonstrated through Ramsay assay with genetic manipulation shown in Figure 6F.

claim: HEK293T cells expressing HA-tagged Gyc76C and Green cGull exhibited dose-dependent increases in fluorescence intensity following ITPa treatment.
source: At 4 min after 50 nM, 250 nM, or 500 nM ITPa treatment, cells expressing HA-tagged Gyc76C and Green cGull exhibited 34%, 88.7%, and 111.4% increases in fluorescence intensity, respectively, indicating a dose-dependent increase in cGMP (Figure 7B-E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated through live-cell imaging assay shown in Figures 7B-E.

claim: Control cells transfected with only Green cGull failed to demonstrate a clear dose-dependent response to ITPa.
source: The same measurements in control cells transfected with only Green cGull failed to demonstrate a clear dose-dependent response with respective increases of 17.5%, 39.8%, and 28.2% (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated through live-cell imaging assay shown in Figure 7.

claim: L-NSCITP are more active in both males and females that were desiccated compared to flies that were kept under normal conditions.
source: In agreement with our prediction, L-NSCITP are more active (indicated by increased GFP immunofluorescence) in both males (Figure 8A) and females (Figure 8B) that were desiccated compared to flies that were kept under normal conditions.
evidence: Demonstrated through CaLexA reporter assay shown in Figures 8A and B.

claim: L-NSCITP activity returned to normal levels in rehydrated flies that were previously exposed to desiccation.
source: Moreover, L-NSCITP activity returned to normal levels in rehydrated flies that were previously exposed to desiccation (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: Demonstrated through CaLexA reporter assay shown in Figures 8A and B.

claim: Reduced ITPa immunofluorescence was observed in ITPa-expressing NSC as well as clock neurons in both males and females that had been exposed to desiccation stress.
source: We observed reduced fluorescence in ITPa-expressing NSC as well as clock neurons in both males (Figure 8C) and females (Figure 8D) that had been exposed to desiccation stress.
evidence: Demonstrated through ITPa immunofluorescence measurements shown in Figures 8C and D.

claim: ITPa immunofluorescence returned to normal levels in desiccated flies that were then allowed to rehydrate.
source: ITPa immunofluorescence returned to normal levels in desiccated flies that were then allowed to rehydrate.
evidence: Demonstrated through ITPa immunofluorescence measurements shown in Figures 8C and D.

claim: ITP knockdown resulted in reduced desiccation tolerance.
source: In agreement with the anti-diuretic effects of ITPa ex vivo, ITP knockdown resulted in reduced desiccation tolerance (Figure 9B).
evidence: Demonstrated through desiccation tolerance assay shown in Figure 9B.

claim: ITP knockdown resulted in reduced water retention.
source: This is likely a result of reduced water retention (Figure 9C) and increased defecation (Figure 9D).
evidence: Demonstrated through water content measurement shown in Figure 9C.

claim: ITP knockdown resulted in increased defecation.
source: This is likely a result of reduced water retention (Figure 9C) and increased defecation (Figure 9D).
evidence: Demonstrated through defecation assay shown in Figure 9D.

claim: ITP knockdown flies exhibited reduced survival under starvation.
source: Females with ITP knockdown exhibited reduced survival under starvation (Figure 9F), prompting us to assess their circulating and stored macronutrients.
evidence: Demonstrated through starvation survival assay shown in Figure 9F.

claim: ITP knockdown flies displayed significantly lower circulating glucose.
source: As expected based on lowered starvation tolerance, these flies displayed significantly lower circulating glucose (Figure 9G) and lipid stores in the fat body (Figure 9I and J).
evidence: Demonstrated through glucose assay shown in Figure 9G.

claim: ITP knockdown flies displayed lower lipid stores in the fat body.
source: As expected based on lowered starvation tolerance, these flies displayed significantly lower circulating glucose (Figure 9G) and lipid stores in the fat body (Figure 9I and J).
evidence: Demonstrated through lipid assay shown in Figures 9I and J.

claim: Glycogen levels remained unaltered in ITP knockdown flies compared to controls.
source: Glycogen levels, however, remained unaltered compared to controls (Figure 9H).
evidence: Demonstrated through glycogen assay shown in Figure 9H.

claim: The size of the ovaries was reduced in ITP knockdown females.
source: As a consequence of these depleted energy reserves, the size of the ovaries was reduced in ITP knockdown females (Figure 9K).
evidence: Demonstrated through ovary imaging shown in Figure 9K.

claim: ITP knockdown flies consumed more food than controls.
source: Surprisingly, the reduction in energy reserves was not attributable to decreased food intake. On the contrary, ITP knockdown flies consumed more food than controls (Figure 9L).
evidence: Demonstrated through feeding assay shown in Figure 9L.

claim: Starved ITP knockdown flies did not display a shift in preference towards nutritive sugars.
source: While fed flies of both the control and experimental genotypes showed no preference (Figure 9M), starved control flies exhibited a shift towards caloric nutritive sugars (Figure 9N), which reflects their drive to restore energy balance. In contrast, starved ITP knockdown flies did not display this shift in preference towards nutritive sugars (Figure 9N), indicating a disruption in the integration of internal metabolic cues with taste-driven food selection.
evidence: Demonstrated through food preference assay shown in Figure 9N.

claim: ITPa overexpression improves desiccation tolerance.
source: In agreement with our ex vivo secretion data, ITPa overexpression improves desiccation tolerance (Figure 10B), likely due to increased water retention, since flies overexpressing ITPa had higher body water content (Figure 10C) and bloated abdomens (Figure 10D).
evidence: Demonstrated through desiccation tolerance assay shown in Figure 10B.

claim: Flies overexpressing ITPa had higher body water content.
source: In agreement with our ex vivo secretion data, ITPa overexpression improves desiccation tolerance (Figure 10B), likely due to increased water retention, since flies overexpressing ITPa had higher body water content (Figure 10C) and bloated abdomens (Figure 10D).
evidence: Demonstrated through water content measurement shown in Figure 10C.

claim: Flies with ITPa overexpression survive longer under starvation.
source: With regard to metabolic physiology, flies with ITPa overexpression survive longer under starvation (Figure 10E).
evidence: Demonstrated through starvation survival assay shown in Figure 10E.

claim: Flies with ITPa overexpression had reduced glucose levels.
source: These flies had reduced glucose levels (Figure 10F) but their glycogen levels were unaltered (Figure 10G).
evidence: Demonstrated through glucose assay shown in Figure 10F.

claim: ITPa overexpression led to increased lipid levels.
source: ITPa overexpression also led to increased lipid levels (Figure 10H).
evidence: Demonstrated through lipid assay shown in Figure 10H.

claim: Flies with ITPa overexpression showed defects in preference between nutritive versus non-nutritive sugar.
source: In addition, flies with ITPa overexpression showed defects in preference between nutritive versus non-nutritive sugar (Figure 10I and J) and had larger ovaries (Figure 10K).
evidence: Demonstrated through food preference assay shown in Figures 10I and J.

claim: Flies with ITPa overexpression had larger ovaries.
source: In addition, flies with ITPa overexpression showed defects in preference between nutritive versus non-nutritive sugar (Figure 10I and J) and had larger ovaries (Figure 10K).
evidence: Demonstrated through ovary imaging shown in Figure 10K.

claim: Flies with Gyc76C knockdown in the MTs exhibit reduced tolerance to desiccation irrespective of the cell type, principal or stellate, being targeted.
source: As expected, flies with Gyc76C knockdown in the MTs exhibit reduced tolerance to desiccation irrespective of the cell type, principal or stellate, being targeted (Figure 11A and D).
evidence: Demonstrated through desiccation tolerance assay shown in Figures 11A and D.

claim: Principal cell knockdown of Gyc76C led to increased survival under salt stress.
source: Interestingly, salt stress impacted flies differently depending on the cell type in which Gyc76C was knocked down. Principal cell knockdown led to increased survival (Figure 11B), whereas stellate cell knockdown resulted in reduced survival (Figure 11E), which could reflect functional differences between the two cell types.
evidence: Demonstrated through salt stress tolerance assay shown in Figure 11B.

claim: Stellate cell knockdown of Gyc76C resulted in reduced survival under salt stress.
source: Interestingly, salt stress impacted flies differently depending on the cell type in which Gyc76C was knocked down. Principal cell knockdown led to increased survival (Figure 11B), whereas stellate cell knockdown resulted in reduced survival (Figure 11E), which could reflect functional differences between the two cell types.
evidence: Demonstrated through salt stress tolerance assay shown in Figure 11E.

claim: Gyc76C knockdown in either MT cell type increased the time taken to recover from chill-coma.
source: Lastly, Gyc76C knockdown in either MT cell type increased the time taken to recover from chill-coma, highlighting deficits in the ability to maintain ionic homeostasis (Figure 11C and F).
evidence: Demonstrated through chill-coma recovery assay shown in Figures 11C and F.

claim: Flies with Gyc76C knockdown in the fat body exhibit a drastic reduction in starvation tolerance compared to control flies.
source: Flies with Gyc76C knockdown in the fat body exhibit a drastic reduction in starvation tolerance compared to control flies (Figure 12A).
evidence: Demonstrated through starvation survival assay shown in Figure 12A.

claim: Gyc76C knockdown flies have lower hemolymph glucose.
source: In agreement with reduced starvation survival, Gyc76C knockdown flies have lower hemolymph glucose (Figure 12B), unaltered glycogen levels (Figure 12C), and lower lipids in the fat body (Figure 12D and E) compared to controls.
evidence: Demonstrated through glucose assay shown in Figure 12B.

claim: Gyc76C knockdown flies have lower lipids in the fat body.
source: In agreement with reduced starvation survival, Gyc76C knockdown flies have lower hemolymph glucose (Figure 12B), unaltered glycogen levels (Figure 12C), and lower lipids in the fat body (Figure 12D and E) compared to controls.
evidence: Demonstrated through lipid assay shown in Figures 12D and E.

claim: Gyc76C knockdown flies fed more than controls.
source: Interestingly, the reduction in energy stores is not due to decreased food intake because Gyc76C knockdown flies fed more than controls (Figure 12F).
evidence: Demonstrated through feeding assay shown in Figure 12F.

claim: Gyc76C knockdown flies preferred yeast over sucrose.
source: In addition, these flies displayed altered food preferences. Specifically, they preferred yeast over sucrose (Figure 12G), possibly to mitigate protein or general caloric deficits since the protein in yeast yields greater caloric value than sugar.
evidence: Demonstrated through food preference assay shown in Figure 12G.

claim: Starved Gyc76C knockdown flies displayed a slight preference for non-nutritive sugar over nutritive sugar.
source: While there was no preference for nutritive or non-nutritive sugar in fed flies (Figure 12H), control flies showed increased preference for nutritive sugar during starvation (Figure 12I). Conversely, starved Gyc76C knockdown flies displayed a slight preference for non-nutritive sugar over nutritive sugar (Figure 12I), suggesting disrupted integration of taste signals with the internal metabolic state.
evidence: Demonstrated through food preference assay shown in Figure 12I.

claim: Flies with Gyc76C knockdown in the fat body have smaller ovaries.
source: We first observed that Gyc76C knockdown flies had drastically shrunken ovaries (Figure 12J).
evidence: Demonstrated through ovary imaging shown in Figure 12J.

claim: Gyc76C knockdown flies defecated more than controls.
source: In addition, knockdown flies also defecated more than controls (Figure 12K) and relatedly had a lower water content (Figure 12L).
evidence: Demonstrated through defecation assay shown in Figure 12K.

claim: Gyc76C knockdown flies had a lower water content.
source: In addition, knockdown flies also defecated more than controls (Figure 12K) and relatedly had a lower water content (Figure 12L).
evidence: Demonstrated through water content measurement shown in Figure 12L.

claim: Gyc76C knockdown flies have reduced DILP2 peptide levels.
source: Therefore, we quantified DILP2 and ITPa peptide levels in the brain NSC following knockdown of Gyc76C in the fat body. Indeed, knockdown flies have reduced DILP2 peptide levels (Figure 12M and O).
evidence: Demonstrated through immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figures 12M and O.

claim: No differences in ITPa peptide levels in L-NSCITP were observed following Gyc76C knockdown in the fat body.
source: However, we did not observe any differences in ITPa peptide levels in L-NSCITP (Figure 12N and O).
evidence: Demonstrated through immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figures 12N and O.

claim: Flies with Gyc76C knockdown in the fat body displayed reduced daytime activity when kept under either fed or starved conditions for one day.
source: Flies with Gyc76C knockdown in the fat body displayed reduced daytime activity when kept under either fed or starved conditions for one day (Figure 12P–R).
evidence: Demonstrated through locomotor activity monitoring shown in Figures 12P-R.

claim: LNdITP and 5th-LNv displayed numerous input and output synapses in the brain.
source: LNdITP and 5th-LNv displayed numerous input and output synapses in the brain (Figure 13B, Figure 13—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated through connectomics analysis shown in Figure 13B.

claim: Both LNdITP and 5th-LNv receive inputs and provide outputs to a broad range of neurons.
source: Consistent with the high number of synapses, both LNdITP and 5th-LNv receive inputs and provide outputs to a broad range of neurons (Figure 13C and D).
evidence: Demonstrated through connectomics analysis shown in Figures 13C and D.

claim: Both LNdITP and 5th-LNv are upstream of at least one pair of DH31-expressing NSC (L-NSCDH31).
source: In addition, both cell types are upstream of at least one pair of DH31-expressing NSC (L-NSCDH31) (Figure 13D).
evidence: Demonstrated through connectomics analysis shown in Figure 13D.

claim: LNdITP receive indirect inputs from VP1l thermo/hygrosensory neurons.
